# Baruch Chapter 6 — Disagreement Log
## [The Letter of Jeremiah]

**Date:** 2026-03-17
**Chapter:** Baruch 6 / Letter of Jeremiah (72 verses)
**Agents:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Total Disagreements:** 22

---

## Disagreement 001 — v.1: Introduction framing

**EMET:** "A copy of the letter that Jeremiah sent to those who were to be led captive"
**LOGOS:** "A copy of the letter that Jeremiah sent to those who were about to be led captive"
**PNEUMA:** "This is a copy of the letter that Jeremiah sent to the Judeans who were about to be marched off to Babylon"
**Issue:** PNEUMA adds "Judeans" (not in the Greek) and "marched off" (more dramatic). LOGOS "about to be" is slightly more natural than EMET "were to be." PNEUMA also adds "This is" as an opener. Consensus: LOGOS without PNEUMA's additions.

---

## Disagreement 002 — v.4: "inspiring awe" vs. "filling with awe" vs. "filling with terror"

**EMET:** "inspiring awe among the nations"
**LOGOS:** "filling the nations with awe"
**PNEUMA:** "filling the nations with terror"
**Issue:** Greek ekphobizonta ta ethnē = striking fear/awe into the nations. The word contains phobos (fear). "Terror" (PNEUMA) may be too strong; "awe" may be too reverent. Context shows this is false fear, which the letter seeks to dispel. Consensus: "filling the nations with awe" — the awe is precisely what is unwarranted.

---

## Disagreement 003 — v.6: "say in your heart" vs. "say to yourself"

**EMET:** "say in your heart: You are the one who should be worshipped, O Lord"
**LOGOS:** "say in your heart: It is you, O Lord, who must be worshipped"
**PNEUMA:** "say to yourself: You alone, O Lord, deserve to be worshipped"
**Issue:** Greek eipate en tais kardiais hymōn = say in your hearts. The inwardness of worship ("in your heart") is important — the Israelites must maintain their faith silently amid external pressure. PNEUMA loses "in your heart." Consensus: "say in your heart."

---

## Disagreement 004 — v.7: "lives" vs. "souls"

**EMET:** "watching over your lives"
**LOGOS:** "watching over your souls"
**PNEUMA:** "watching over your lives"
**Issue:** Greek psychas hymōn = your souls/lives. In LXX Greek psychē = the whole person, often rendered "lives" in English. "Souls" has a more spiritual connotation; "lives" is more concrete. Consensus: "souls" — the protection is not merely physical; it is the total person in exile.

---

## Disagreement 005 — v.8: "polished" vs. "polished smooth"

**EMET:** "their tongues have been polished by a craftsman"
**LOGOS:** "their tongues have been polished smooth by a craftsman"
**PNEUMA:** "their tongues were shaped smooth by a craftsman"
**Issue:** Greek xestos = smoothed/polished/planed. All agents agree on the basic meaning. The idol's tongue is polished metal — it looks like it should speak but cannot. "Polished" is sufficient. Consensus: "polished by a craftsman."

---

## Disagreement 006 — v.9: Simile structure — girl with jewelry

**EMET:** "as for an offering to them of gold as if for a girl who loves ornaments"
**LOGOS:** "people bring gold as an offering to them as they would to a girl who loves jewelry"
**PNEUMA:** "People bring them gold offerings as you would deck out a girl who loves jewelry"
**Issue:** Greek hōsper kosmountai parthenos philokosmē = like adorning a girl who loves adornment. The comparison is to adorning rather than giving. LOGOS adds "as they would to a girl" (gift-giving); PNEUMA "deck out" (adorning) is closer to the Greek. Consensus: between LOGOS and PNEUMA — "people bring gold as an offering, as one would adorn a girl who loves jewelry."

---

## Disagreement 007 — v.11: "temple rooftop" vs. "roof of the temple"

**EMET:** "prostitutes on the roof of the temple"
**LOGOS:** "prostitutes on the temple rooftop"
**PNEUMA:** "prostitutes who work the temple roof"
**Issue:** PNEUMA "work the temple roof" adds interpretive framing ("work" suggests their profession). The Greek simply says "prostitutes on the roof of the temple." Consensus: "prostitutes on the roof of the temple."

---

## Disagreement 008 — v.14-15: The armed but helpless judge — structure

**EMET:** "He who cannot put to death anyone who sins against him wields a scepter like a judge"
**LOGOS:** "He who cannot put to death anyone who wrongs him wields a scepter like a judge"
**PNEUMA:** "One of them holds a scepter as if he were a judge over the country — but he cannot put to death anyone who wrongs him"
**Issue:** PNEUMA reorders to put the observation ("holds a scepter") before the critique ("cannot put to death"). The Greek order is critique first, then the image. EMET/LOGOS preserve the Greek order. Consensus: LOGOS order.

---

## Disagreement 009 — v.16: The first refrain — exact wording

**EMET:** "From this it is evident that they are not gods; so do not fear them."
**LOGOS:** "From this it is evident that they are not gods; so do not fear them."
**PNEUMA:** "From all this it is plain: they are not gods. Do not fear them."
**Issue:** EMET and LOGOS agree exactly. PNEUMA adds "all" and changes punctuation. The refrain should be consistent in its first appearance. Consensus: "From this it is evident that they are not gods; so do not fear them."

---

## Disagreement 010 — v.17: "vessel... useless when broken" comparison

**EMET:** "just as a vessel that a man uses is of no use when it is broken"
**LOGOS:** "just as a man's vessel is made useless when it is broken"
**PNEUMA:** "A broken vessel is no use to anyone"
**Issue:** Greek hōs skeuous anthrōpou chrēsimou suntribentos = as a useful vessel of a man being broken. PNEUMA simplifies and loses the man/vessel parallel with man/idol. Consensus: LOGOS phrasing.

---

## Disagreement 011 — v.20: "wooden beam" — description of the idol

**EMET:** "like a beam of the house; men say their hearts are eaten away"
**LOGOS:** "like a wooden beam in the house; they say the hearts within them are eaten out"
**PNEUMA:** "like a wooden roof-beam... when the worms come up from the ground and gnaw at them and their clothing, they don't even notice"
**Issue:** PNEUMA adds "roof-beam" (specifying "roof") and "worms come up from the ground" (though this is in v.20b in the Greek: ta herpeta tēs gēs esthiei autous). PNEUMA's expansion incorporates elements from the verse without adding foreign material. Consensus: more compact rendering per LOGOS.

---

## Disagreement 012 — v.22: Animal enumeration

**EMET:** "Bats and swallows and the birds alight on their bodies and heads; and cats do likewise."
**LOGOS:** "Bats, swallows, and birds settle on their bodies and heads; and so do cats."
**PNEUMA:** "Bats, swallows, and birds roost on their heads and bodies. Cats too."
**Issue:** All agree on the animals. "Alight" (EMET) vs. "settle" (LOGOS) vs. "roost" (PNEUMA). "Perch/settle" is most neutral. Consensus: "settle on their bodies and heads."

---

## Disagreement 013 — v.25: "without regard to price" vs. "for any price"

**EMET:** "bought without regard to price"
**LOGOS:** "purchased without regard to price"
**PNEUMA:** "sold for any price"
**Issue:** Greek agorazontai = they are bought. "Without regard to price" means they are not treated as valuables (the irony is that people buy them but they are worthless). PNEUMA "sold for any price" reverses the perspective from buyer to seller, which changes the satirical point. Consensus: "purchased without regard to price."

---

## Disagreement 014 — v.28: Wives salting the sacrificial meat

**EMET:** "their wives salt some of it, but they give none of it to the poor or helpless"
**LOGOS:** "their wives also preserve some of it in brine, but give nothing to the poor or helpless"
**PNEUMA:** "Their wives take home some of the meat and salt it — but not a scrap goes to the poor or the helpless"
**Issue:** Greek halizousin = they salt. "Preserve in brine" (LOGOS) is interpretively accurate. "Salt it" is simpler. PNEUMA adds "not a scrap." Consensus: "their wives also salt some of it, but give nothing to the poor or the helpless."

---

## Disagreement 015 — v.30: Women as officiants — rhetorical question structure

**EMET:** "Because women serve as officiants at the shrines of the wooden, silvered, and golden gods"
**LOGOS:** "Women serve as officiants at the shrines of these wooden, silvered, and golden gods"
**PNEUMA:** "These wooden, silvered, and gilded things have women officiating at their shrines"
**Issue:** EMET preserves the question/answer structure ("For how can they be called gods? Because..."). LOGOS and PNEUMA restructure. The question-answer rhythm is rhetorically important. Consensus: EMET structure with minor polish.

---

## Disagreement 016 — v.43: The temple women with cords — rendering the scene

**EMET:** "Women with cords around them sit along the roads, burning bran for incense"
**LOGOS:** "The women, wearing cords around them, sit in the streets burning bran as incense"
**PNEUMA:** "There are women who sit along the roads wearing cords around their waists, burning bran as incense"
**Issue:** PNEUMA adds "around their waists" (the Greek says simply "cords around them"). The practice described is the Herodotean sacred prostitution of Babylon (Histories 1.199). The cord is cut when a stranger selects the woman. All agents render the scene accurately. Consensus: LOGOS phrasing.

---

## Disagreement 017 — v.46: "cannot live very long" — the craftsmen's mortality

**EMET:** "Those who make them can hardly live long"
**LOGOS:** "Those who make them cannot themselves live very long"
**PNEUMA:** "the craftsmen themselves don't live very long"
**Issue:** Greek gar oudeis dynēsetai autoi zōn chronia = for none of them will be able to live long. The rhetorical point: the craftsman dies; his creation is therefore not immortal. All agents agree. Consensus: LOGOS phrasing.

---

## Disagreement 018 — v.53: "like crows between heaven and earth"

**EMET:** "they are like crows between heaven and earth"
**LOGOS:** "they are like crows between heaven and earth"
**PNEUMA:** "They are like crows drifting between sky and ground"
**Issue:** All agree on "crows." PNEUMA adds "drifting" and changes "heaven" to "sky." The image is of creatures that belong nowhere — neither gods (heaven) nor earthly authorities (earth). "Heaven" preserves the theological register. Consensus: "like crows between heaven and earth."

---

## Disagreement 019 — v.54: "burned like timbers" vs. "burned like beams"

**EMET:** "they will be burned in the midst like beams"
**LOGOS:** "they themselves are burned there like timbers"
**PNEUMA:** "the idol gets burned along with the beams"
**Issue:** PNEUMA "along with the beams" changes the comparison: in PNEUMA the idol is burned alongside beams (not as beams); in EMET/LOGOS the idol is burned like timbers — because it IS timber. The point of the satire is precisely that the "god" is just wood. Consensus: "they themselves are burned there like timbers."

---

## Disagreement 020 — v.58: Triple better-than comparison

**EMET:** "better to be a king showing his valor, or a household utensil that serves its owner's use, than to be these false gods"
**LOGOS:** "better to be a king showing his valor, or a household vessel that serves its owner's needs, than these false gods"
**PNEUMA:** "a kitchen pot that serves its owner's needs is better than these gods"
**Issue:** PNEUMA condenses the four-part comparison and omits the king. The king comparison is first in the Greek and should not be omitted. "Household vessel" (LOGOS) vs. "utensil" (EMET) vs. "kitchen pot" (PNEUMA). Consensus: LOGOS phrasing with all four comparisons.

---

## Disagreement 021 — v.69: "scarecrow in a cucumber field"

**EMET:** "like a scarecrow in a cucumber field that protects nothing"
**LOGOS:** "like a scarecrow in a cucumber patch that guards nothing"
**PNEUMA:** "They are like a scarecrow in a cucumber field — protecting nothing"
**Issue:** Greek prosōpō en sikuērati = as a face/scarecrow in a cucumber garden. "Cucumber field" vs. "cucumber patch" — minor. "Protects nothing" vs. "guards nothing." All agree on the image. Consensus: "like a scarecrow in a cucumber field that guards nothing."

---

## Disagreement 022 — v.72: Final verse — "upright person" vs. "righteous man"

**EMET:** "the righteous man who has no idols"
**LOGOS:** "an upright person who has no idols"
**PNEUMA:** "an honest person with no idols"
**Issue:** Greek anthrōpos dikaios = a righteous/just person. "Righteous" (EMET) is the standard LXX translation; "upright" is more neutral; "honest" (PNEUMA) is too weak. The letter closes by contrasting the shame-free life of the righteous person with the reproach clinging to idol-worshippers. Consensus: "the upright person who has no idols" — dikaios is weighty enough to deserve more than "honest" but "upright" is more accessible than "righteous" at the close of a satirical letter.
